title: Guest post: Why tough methane cuts are crucial for keeping warming ‘well-below’ 2C - Carbon Brief
gist: A study in Communications Earth & Environment decouples methane from CO2 and shows that even the most ambitious existing national net-zero targets deliver peak warming above 1.85C without stringent methane cuts, and that current policies — which imply methane emissions rising about 20% by 2050 — push peak warming above 2C even if global CO2 hits net-zero by 2050. It also finds the standard 2C remaining carbon budget of 1,000-1,150GtCO2 silently assumes 27-35% methane cuts, and shrinks by roughly 30% to about 750GtCO2 under a GWP* framing.

insights.claim: Even under the most ambitious existing national net-zero targets, an absence of methane reduction produces peak warming above 1.85C relative to pre-industrial levels — beyond what has been argued as consistent with the Paris Agreement's 'well-below' 2C limit.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: CO2-only net-zero pledges are structurally insufficient on their own terms, so expect methane-specific targets to become the next disclosure and regulatory frontier for oil and gas, agriculture and waste operators.

insights.claim: Under current policies methane emissions are expected to rise about 20% by 2050 relative to 2020, a pathway that produces peak warming above 2C even if global CO2 emissions reach net-zero by that same date.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The single most consequential number in the piece: the current methane trajectory alone breaks 2C regardless of CO2 success, making methane abatement policy the highest-leverage regulatory risk to watch.

insights.claim: Holding peak warming to 1.7C alongside a 2050 net-zero CO2 target requires methane emissions to fall at least 69% by 2050 relative to 2020, or 63% if the 2050 net-zero target covers all greenhouse gases.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Puts a hard, quantified abatement requirement on livestock, landfill and fossil-fuel methane that far exceeds any pledge now in force — a demand signal for detection, capture and low-methane agriculture technology.

insights.claim: For several combinations of net-zero date and peak warming level there is no compatible methane mitigation target at all — no feasible methane pathway delivers 1.7C peak warming if net-zero CO2 arrives in 2060 or 2100.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Certain temperature-and-timing combinations in corporate and national plans are arithmetically impossible; a useful screen for identifying targets that cannot be met by any abatement mix.

insights.claim: A 2C peak warming outcome tolerates methane emissions rising 8% by 2050 under a 2050 net-zero CO2 target, but demands an 83% cut if net-zero CO2 slips to 2100 — showing that methane requirements tighten sharply as CO2 action is delayed.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Methane and CO2 timing are substitutes with a brutal exchange rate; delay on decarbonisation converts directly into near-impossible methane obligations later.

insights.claim: The commonly cited remaining carbon budget of roughly 1,000-1,150GtCO2 for 2C as of 2025, drawn from the IPCC's 2021 report and a 2023 Nature study, is founded on an unstated assumption of 27-35% methane cuts by 2050 relative to 2020.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The headline carbon budget used across net-zero planning is conditional on methane action nobody has committed to — a hidden dependency that makes the budget less bankable than it appears.

insights.claim: Under a GWP* framing, where methane is cut only enough to maintain 'no additional warming', the best estimate of the remaining 2C carbon budget shrinks by around 30% to approximately 750GtCO2.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Choosing GWP* — favoured by agricultural lobbies as it lightens livestock methane obligations — costs roughly 300GtCO2 of CO2 headroom, transferring the burden onto energy and industry.

insights.claim: If methane emissions are never cut, the remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.7C has in effect already been exhausted.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Removes 1.7C from the feasible set absent methane action, which strengthens the case that peak-warming outcomes hinge on non-CO2 gases rather than on energy transition speed alone.

insights.claim: Because methane and CO2 have different atmospheric lifetimes and warming properties, any CO2-equivalent conversion is only valid for a chosen time horizon and baseline, and the assumptions baked into the calculation can make methane mitigation look either like an immediate priority or almost unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Metric selection is effectively a policy decision disguised as accounting; scrutinise which GWP convention underlies any corporate methane claim before valuing its abatement.
insights.quote: Depending on the assumptions baked into calculations, methane mitigation can either appear as an immediate priority or framed as almost unnecessary.

insights.claim: The three competing conversion metrics diverge sharply in what they demand: GWP20 emphasises urgent methane cuts but implicitly discounts future damages, GWP100 weights long-term warming and is the standard for UN national reporting, integrated assessment models and the corporate GHG Protocol, while GWP* counts emission rates so that very limited methane reductions bring CO2-equivalent emissions to zero.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A single accounting-standard change from GWP100 to GWP* could wipe out most reported methane liability for livestock and gas producers without changing a molecule — a live standard-setting risk to monitor.

insights.claim: Asking how much methane corresponds to one tonne of CO2 is framed as being as difficult as asking how much spaghetti equals a chicken — each comparison metric is convenient but valid only for that specific comparison.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A memorable framing for challenging any single-number CO2-equivalent claim in a disclosure or offset product.
insights.quote: no amount of spaghetti is the same as a chicken
insights.locator: The question is as difficult to answer

insights.claim: Because integrated assessment models combine CO2 and methane emissions, the impact of methane cuts alone cannot be isolated in existing emissions scenarios, which is why the study builds a separate scenario space treating the two gases as independent.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Standard scenario libraries cannot answer the methane question directly, so any methane-specific valuation built on off-the-shelf IAM scenarios is inferring rather than measuring.

insights.claim: Integrated assessment models only represent cost-effective combinations of CO2 and methane mitigation, excluding the messy, non-cost-optimal pathways that real-world climate policy actually follows.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Official scenarios systematically understate the cost and overstate the elegance of real decarbonisation — a reason to treat IAM-derived cost curves as optimistic lower bounds.
insights.quote: climate policy is messy and emission pathways are rarely cost-effective in the real world

insights.claim: Only a handful of countries — including Japan, Mexico and South Korea — specify methane mitigation targets at all.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Methane policy is a near-greenfield regulatory area; first-mover jurisdictions signal where compliance markets for methane abatement technology emerge first.

insights.claim: Cutting methane emissions by around one-third, in line with the Global Methane Pledge target for 2030, could reduce peak warming by 0.15C, of which 0.05C is deliverable through interventions that come at no net cost according to the IEA.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A third of the pledge's warming benefit is free money — leak detection and capture in oil and gas remain the cheapest tenth-of-a-degree available, and the gap between free and delivered abatement is the policy failure to watch.

insights.claim: Methane traps heat far more efficiently than CO2 but fades from the atmosphere after just a few decades, making it the highest-leverage lever available for limiting warming in the near term and the second-largest contributor to global warming after CO2.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Short atmospheric lifetime means methane action pays off within a single investment horizon rather than over a century — the strongest argument for near-term abatement capital in agriculture, gas and waste.
insights.locator: Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas

insights.claim: The study proposes inverting standard practice: rather than choosing a CO2-equivalent conversion, states and organisations should first set a peak global warming limit and then derive the minimum compatible methane reduction target from their existing net-zero date.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A ready-made audit method for testing whether any company or country target is physically coherent — apply the net-zero year and the claimed temperature limit and read off the implied methane cut.
